blocks.text: Dear Mr. Martin:

Thank you for asking us to find your next vice president of engineering. The conversations that brought us here were good ones, and we come away with a clear sense of what the role has to carry at {{fact:f:E-2016-001.client}} over the next few years. This letter sets down what we have agreed, so that the two of us work from the same understanding and not from memory.
Please read it against those conversations. If any part of it sits differently from what you understood, say so before you sign, and we will put it right.
The Assignment

Northgate will conduct a retained search for a vice president of engineering at {{fact:f:E-2016-001.client}}, reporting to you. The search runs against a written position specification that we prepare with you and that you approve before we approach anyone. That document governs the assignment. If the market tells us something the specification did not anticipate, and on a role of this kind it usually does, we bring it back to you and amend the specification openly instead of quietly widening the brief.

The engagement is retained rather than contingent, and the distinction matters to how we will behave. What you are buying is a market covered properly and to a standard, including the part of it that turns out to hold nobody worth your time. We will not send you a resume to show activity.
How the Search Will Run
The work moves through five stages:

items: 1. Specification. We meet the people this executive will work with most closely, and we write the specification for your approval.
2. Research. We map the companies and the roles where a person of this description is likely to sit today, and we build a target list off that map.
3. Approach and assessment. We contact the people on the list and interview the ones worth interviewing, in person wherever the calendar allows it.
4. Slate. We present a short list with a written appraisal of each candidate, and we manage your interview process from there.
5. References and close. We take references, help you shape the offer, and stay with the search until your candidate has accepted and given notice.

blocks.text: In practice the stages overlap, and research continues while the first approaches are underway. You will hear from us on a regular cycle, and each report will tell you how many people we have approached, how many are in live conversation, and where the market is pushing back. Where it pushes back on something in the specification, we will say so early, while there is still time to do something about it.
Your Team

Jeffrey Patterson will carry the search day to day and is the person to call about anything of substance. He came up through our research side, and it shows in his habits: he will not put a name in front of you until he can say precisely why it belongs there.

James Grant, a senior consultant here, works the assignment alongside him and will sit in on your interviews. John Chang handles the research behind the target list, the scheduling, and the written record of our sessions with you. I read everything that goes out to you under our name, and you are welcome to come to me directly at any point in the search.
Fees and Payment

Our fee for the assignment is {{fact:f:E-2016-001.fee}}. It is fixed at the outset and is not calculated from the compensation you eventually agree with your candidate, which keeps our advice on that compensation disinterested. We will invoice the fee in three equal installments: the first on commencement, the second when we present the slate, and the third when your candidate accepts. Invoices are payable within thirty days of receipt.

Expenses sit outside the fee and are billed at cost. They are candidate and consultant travel, and any research we commission from outside the firm. We will agree anything material with you before we incur it, and the detail appears on the invoice.
Term and Termination

The engagement begins {{fact:f:E-2016-001.start}} and we expect it to run about seven months from that date through to a signed acceptance. Either of us may end it on thirty days' written notice. If you end it, you owe us the installments already due and the expenses already committed on your behalf, and nothing beyond that.
If the executive we place leaves within twelve months, for any reason other than a change you make to the role or the terms of it, we will conduct one replacement search for expenses only.
Confidentiality

Everything we learn about {{fact:f:E-2016-001.client}} in the course of the work we hold in confidence and use only for this search. We ask the same of you for what we tell you about candidates, and here we will press the point. Most of the people we approach are content where they are and take a real risk in talking to us. Their names stay inside the interview process, they do not appear in anything that circulates, and we will not confirm to anyone outside it that a particular person is in conversation with you.
For the term of the engagement and for one year after it closes, we will not approach the executive we place, or any member of your leadership team, for another client.
Limitation of Liability

We will do this work with the care and skill you are entitled to expect. We verify what a candidate tells us about their record, and we will tell you plainly what we could not verify. The hiring decision is yours, and we give no warranty as to how anyone you employ will perform in the role. Our liability under this agreement is limited to the fees paid under it, except where the law does not permit that limit.
Governing Law

This agreement is governed by the law of the state in which our office is established, and any dispute arising under it belongs in that state's courts. If any provision of the letter is found unenforceable, the remainder stands.

If this reflects our understanding, please sign both copies and return one to me. The next step after that is a short one: Jeffrey Patterson will call your office to fix the specification meetings for the first week of the engagement, and we would like the two people this role will work with most closely in the room for one of them.

To: James Grant; John Chang
From: Jeffrey Patterson, Research Consultant
Re: VP Engineering search for {{fact:f:E-2016-001.client}}, kickoff and plan

The thing that will decide this search is the research, so that is where the weight of our effort goes in the opening weeks. The people who can run an engineering organization through the platform work {{fact:f:E-2016-001.client}} has ahead of it are almost all employed and none of them are reading job advertisements. We will have to find them, and then we will have to give them a reason to take the call.

For the record: the engagement began {{fact:f:E-2016-001.start}} and runs about seven months. Michael Martin, the chief operating officer, is our client on it, and the role reports to him. He is direct, he answers quickly, and he has told us he would rather see four candidates he can argue about than eight he cannot tell apart.
What the client is actually buying

A vice president of engineering who has done this at the size the company is growing into, not the size it is now. That is the whole brief, and every judgment we make about a prospect comes back to it. Where we are unsure whether someone clears that bar, the answer is to keep looking, not to talk ourselves into the list we have.
How the work divides

items: 1. Specification. I will run the two meetings on site and draft the specification off them. John Chang sits in on both and keeps the record. I want the draft with Michael Martin for approval inside two weeks of the second meeting.

2. Market map. John Chang builds the map: the companies at and just above the client's scale that have done comparable platform work, and the engineering leadership in each. I would rather have a map that is honest about its gaps than one that looks complete.

3. Target list and approaches. James Grant and I split the list by sector once the map is stable. Approaches go out in waves so that we can read the response and adjust the pitch before we have spent the whole market.
4. Assessment. Every prospect who gets past a first call gets a structured interview from one of us in person, with written notes the same day. No exceptions for people we already know.
5. Slate and client process. We present with written appraisals, then manage the client interviews, references, and the offer.

blocks.text: Discipline on names

Nothing that leaves this office names a candidate outside the interview process. In the status notes and the client materials, people are described by the role they hold and the kind of company they hold it in. James Grant is stricter about this than I am and he is right to be; follow his practice, not mine, on anything that goes into a document.
The first three weeks
Three things need to close out before the search is properly moving, and I want each of them owned by name.

items: 1. John Chang to have the specification meetings in the calendar this week, and the first cut of the market map two weeks after that.

2. James Grant to review the off-limits question with me before any approach goes out. Two companies on the obvious target list sit close enough to the client that we should have Michael Martin rule on them instead of leaving us to guess.
3. Me to get the specification approved in writing. Nothing goes to a prospect until it is.

blocks.text: Bring me anything that looks like a problem while it is still small. I will circulate the approved specification the day it comes back from the client, and we start the first wave of approaches that week.
Dear Michael,

The search is on schedule, and the research has turned up more depth in the market than I expected when we drafted the specification. I am starting this thread so that the running record of the search lives in one place; I will send the substantive updates here and copy James Grant and John Chang, who are working the assignment with me.

Where we stand: the specification you approved has gone out to the first wave of prospects, and we are in live conversation with nine people from the map. Two of them run engineering organizations through exactly the kind of platform change you described to me in February. I am not putting names or employers in writing until they have had that conversation inside their own companies, which is normal at this stage and is the reason good people talk to us at all.

There are a couple of things I need from your side. John Chang will look for ninety minutes in your calendar in the next two weeks for a calibration session with James Grant and me, where we walk you through the map and test the specification against what the market has actually said back to us. Separately, three companies on the target list sit close enough to {{fact:f:E-2016-001.client}} that I will not approach anyone there without a ruling from you first. I will send the three names to you directly this week.
Sincerely
VP Engineering Search for {{fact:f:E-2016-001.client}}

A briefing for Michael Martin and his colleagues on where the search stands. The engagement commenced {{fact:f:E-2016-001.start}} and is scoped to run about seven months. This briefing covers the research phase and the approaches now underway.
Where the search stands

items: The position specification is approved and is the document every approach is made against.
The market map is complete for the sectors we agreed, and a second pass is open on two adjacent ones.
The first wave of approaches has gone out; a second wave follows once we have read the response to the first.
A number of conversations are live. None of them are far enough along to name in a document.

blocks.text: What the market has said back

items: The profile exists, but it is concentrated in companies one size larger than yours, which is what we expected and planned for.
The strongest people are not in the market. Each of them needs a reason to move, and the reason is the scope of the role and not the package.
Candidates ask early about the reporting line and about how much of the architecture decision is genuinely theirs. Clear answers there are worth more to us than anything else you can give us.

blocks.text: How we are describing the role

items: As ownership of the engineering organization through a change of platform, not as maintenance of the one you have.
As a seat where the executive is accountable for delivery and for the team that does it.
As a company at the point where the next stage of growth needs an engineering leader who has been there before.

blocks.text: Your team at Northgate

items: Jeffrey Patterson, Research Consultant, carries the search day to day and is your first call.
James Grant, Senior Consultant, works the target list and will sit in on your interviews.
John Chang, Research Associate, holds the market map, the scheduling, and the record of our sessions.

blocks.text: What happens next

items: A calibration session with you, to test the specification against what the market has told us.
Your ruling on the three companies we flagged as too close to {{fact:f:E-2016-001.client}} to approach without it.
Second wave of approaches, then first-round assessment interviews conducted by us.

blocks.text: Working Session: VP Engineering Search for {{fact:f:E-2016-001.client}}

The session was held at the client's offices and ran ninety minutes. Its purpose was to review the interim list and to settle the compensation question before we take the search any further. One decision was reached and two questions were left open. Each is recorded below with the person who owns it.
Present

items: Michael Martin, Chief Operating Officer, {{fact:f:E-2016-001.client}}
Jeffrey Patterson, Research Consultant, Northgate Talent Partners
James Grant, Senior Consultant, Northgate Talent Partners
John Chang, Research Associate, Northgate Talent Partners

blocks.text: The interim list

Jeffrey Patterson took the meeting through the seven prospects currently in conversation, describing each by their present role and the scale of the organization they run. Four were assessed as likely to reach the slate. Two are strong on the platform work and thin on the size of team they have carried. One is stronger than the specification asked for and correspondingly less likely to move.
The meeting agreed that the four are enough to build a slate around if one more of comparable weight can be found in the adjacent sectors now being worked.

One prospect who had been in conversation since April withdrew during the week before the session, having been promoted inside their current company. Jeffrey Patterson noted that this is the second withdrawal of that kind on this search, and that both came from the same sector, which may say something about how that sector is currently retaining its engineering leadership.
Compensation

Michael Martin raised the compensation band, which he described as the constraint he is least able to move. James Grant said, and asked that it be recorded, that the band as written will not hold the two strongest people in the current group, and that we should learn that now instead of at offer. He did not press for a decision at the session and accepted that the client needs to take it internally.
It was agreed that {{fact:f:E-2016-001.client}} will come back to us on the band, and that in the meantime we will continue to describe the role by its scope and not by its package.
Discretion

The client asked whether candidates could be identified by name in the papers circulated to his colleagues. Jeffrey Patterson explained our practice, which is that candidates are described by current role until they have told their own employers, and that names enter the written record only once the client interview process begins. The client accepted this without reservation.
The specification

No change to the approved specification was proposed or made. The meeting reviewed the two requirements that have proved hardest to meet together, which are the scale of engineering organization the candidate has run and direct experience of a platform change, and concluded that both should stand. It was noted that the market has so far produced people who are convincing on one or the other more readily than on both.
Decision

The slate will be presented in the second half of June rather than in the first, so that the additional prospect can be assessed properly. The client agreed to hold his own interview dates until the presentation is fixed.
Action items

rows: Take the compensation band internally and return a position on it
Complete the assessment interviews on the two adjacent-sector prospects
Circulate written appraisals of the four likely candidates, by role and without names
Fix the slate presentation date with the client once the band is settled

blocks.text: The next step is the client's position on the compensation band. Everything else in this record waits on it, and the slate date will be fixed within a day of it arriving.
Status Report: VP Engineering Search
Prepared for the leadership team at {{fact:f:E-2016-001.client}}, covering the period since our working session in May. The search is at its midpoint and is on schedule.
Where the search stands

We have a slate. Five candidates have come through our own assessment process, four of them at or above the standard the specification sets, and the fifth strong enough that we would want you to see the comparison. The compensation band, which was the open question in May, has been settled on your side, and the two conversations that were at risk over it have both stayed live as a result. The next material step belongs to you now, not to us.

It is worth recording what the market has cost us to reach that point, because it bears on how the remaining months should be run. We approached seventy-one people across the mapped companies. Thirty-one took a first conversation, nineteen were taken through to a full interview, and five are on the slate. Two prospects withdrew after being promoted where they were, which is the ordinary hazard of a search in a market this tight, and it is the reason we keep a second wave in reserve instead of closing the list early.
Completed in this period

items: 1. We closed the second wave of approaches. The full target list has now been worked, including the three companies you ruled on after the April briefing, two of which you cleared and one of which we have left alone.
2. James Grant completed the assessment interviews in the adjacent sectors, which produced the fifth candidate and eliminated four others.

3. We interviewed every candidate on the slate in person, with written appraisals against the specification rather than against each other. John Chang has those appraisals ready to circulate on the day of the presentation.
4. We began preliminary reference work on the two candidates who have told their own employers they are in a process. For the rest the references wait until you have interviewed them.

blocks.text: The period ahead

items: 1. Slate presentation. Ninety minutes with you and whoever else will interview, taking the candidates one at a time by role and record. Names are given in the room and in the written appraisals, and not before.

2. First-round client interviews, which we schedule and prepare candidates for. Two of the five will need to travel and their availability is genuinely tight; the earlier we hold dates, the less we lose here.
3. Full referencing on whoever you take to a second round, and a verification pass on the record each of them has given us.
4. Offer and close. We will advise on the package and manage the conversation with the candidate through acceptance and notice.

blocks.text: Risks, and where we need you
Three things could cost us time between here and an accepted offer, and each of them sits at least partly on your side of the table, so I set them out before asking for anything.

items: 1. Interview scheduling. A senior person in a live job can hold two or three conversations in a month, not ten. If your interviewers can block dates now, before the presentation, we will protect several weeks of the schedule.
2. Time between rounds. The candidates who impress you will read a long gap as a loss of interest and start listening to other approaches. We would like no more than two weeks between rounds.

3. Counteroffers. Two of the five are people their employers will fight to keep. We prepare candidates for that conversation, but the preparation only works if the offer, when it comes, is decided and not tentative.

blocks.text: Budget

The engagement fee remains {{fact:f:E-2016-001.fee}}, fixed as set out in our agreement, and nothing in the work to date changes it. We will invoice the second of the three installments on presentation of the slate. Expenses to date are limited to candidate travel for two in-person interviews and are running well inside what we would have estimated at this point.
Summary

The search is where it should be at the midpoint: a slate ready, the compensation question closed, and the market worked far enough that we can say with confidence what is in it and what is not. Nothing in the second half of this engagement asks you to take our word for a candidate. You will meet all five, you will have the written appraisals in front of you, and where we could not verify something in a record we will say so in the room.

The one action that moves everything else is fixing the presentation date, and John Chang will call your office this week to do it. If any part of this report raises a question you want to put to me directly, my line is open.

Jeffrey Patterson
Research Consultant
Northgate Talent Partners
